title: The coffee ring effect
hook: A coffee drop dries as a dark ring because the liquid races to its edge.
peek: A spilled drop of coffee dries into a dark ring rather than an even stain. Physicists worked out why in 1997: as the edge dries, liquid flows outward to replace it, carrying the coffee grains along. Whisky, oddly, does not do it.
lede: Spill a drop of coffee on a table and let it dry. Instead of an even brown spot, you get a pale middle with a dark rim. It looks as if the coffee was pushed outward, and it was. In 1997 a team of physicists at the University of Chicago explained it in the journal Nature, and the answer is a flow too slow to notice.

bullets.text: As a drop starts to dry, its edge often sticks in place on the surface. The drop cannot shrink inward, so it flattens instead, losing liquid fastest at the thin rim.
To replace what evaporates at the edge, liquid flows outward from the middle. It carries tiny coffee particles with it, and they pile up along the rim, leaving the dark ring.

In 2011 researchers at the University of Pennsylvania found that stretched, egg-shaped particles largely avoid the ring. They clump together at the surface and settle evenly, while round ones flow to the edge.
In 2016 a Princeton team found that drops of whisky dry into an even film. Flows driven by the alcohol, plus natural substances from the barrel, keep the particles spread out instead.
The effect is a real nuisance for inkjet printing and coatings, where an even layer matters. Understanding it has helped engineers design inks that dry smoothly.
